rv.q: What is surprising is how effective and damn fun it all is.

The Future gradually settles in to an enjoyable-enough thrill park ride, with its special effects, video projections and lighting finally paying off in the final 20 minutes of its nearly three-hour running time.
Though large, it’s less a full-scale new work than a semi-operable souvenir.
If this is the future arriving on Broadway, it looks way too much like another medium’s past.
If this is the future, please send it back.
Alas, the musical constantly makes easier, cheaper choices, dropping its own aesthetic rules if it serves a joke in the moment.
So, in summary: a gifted cast with thankless roles, a hokey book that takes no chances, and an abysmal score that drags everything down.
But the musical as a whole never achieves liftoff, or even the stage equivalent of 88 miles an hour.

On Broadway, however, we have a bloated gizmo nobody asked for that, while enjoyable in parts and with an embraceable star in Casey Likes as Marty, never justifies its perplexing existence as a stage musical.
The Musical just might be one of the most exciting feats of theatricality I have ever seen on stage.
As for the 21-year-old Likes, Back to the Future is a case of getting what you deserve: a starring role in a new Broadway musical hit.
The musical adaptation, now on Broadway with 1.21 gigawatts of spectacle, honors all these views at once and gives Back to the Future the larger-than-life presentation it deserves.
The quality of the show rises to 88 mph whenever he puts in an appearance.

Back to the Future is a night of winning froth—of striking visuals, a few very good performances, and perfectly fine songs—which, just as it emphatically resists examining its more complex contours, also does its dazzling best to ensure those watching do the same.
If you love Back to the Future the film, Back to the Future: The Musical will give you everything you’ve dreamed of.
It’s a safe fun evening, as you’ll know what you’re going to get, with just a little more razzle-dazzles thrown in.
It’s the most innovative aspect of a musical that mostly wallows in the past.
However, those who want to be taken by surprise and offered something new will be vastly disappointed.
They are pretty much the stars of the show—and of course the car should be above the title.
The musical is good at pointing and saying, "Look, something shiny or cool!"
The visuals are what ultimately drive both of these vehicles, as well as America’s obsession with nostalgia and the known and already loved commodity.

cn.t: A crowd-pleasing spectacle that delivers impressive technical effects—especially the flying DeLorean—but critics find it overly faithful to the film, lacking original musical theater magic, with forgettable songs and bloated runtime.

sg.ra: With a 44'10" proscenium and a stage wider than most Broadway houses, Orchestra Center C-G is the only zone where you get the full picture head-on without sacrificing actor-face detail. Spectacle-heavy productions here (BTTF's DeLorean, Mamma Mia! dance numbers) are blocked edge-to-edge, so off-center seats lose pieces even a few rows in.

This is the house's quiet value zone: full center alignment matters more here than proximity does because the auditorium is wider than deep, so row V center still reads front-on. Last orchestra row is short (~6 seats) with unusual legroom per multiple patrons. Tradeoff specific to Winter Garden: the mezzanine overhang starts around row O per published guides, clipping the top of the stage — fine for naturalistic plays, worse for musicals with fly-in sets.

Wide-house penalty hits hardest here: because the auditorium is broader than deep, side-orchestra angles into the stage are sharper than in a typical Broadway house — the further out you sit, the more the upstage far corner disappears. Multiple patrons specifically call out stage-right pillars clipping their view on Salesman; works better for plays where action holds center than for musicals with full-stage choreography.

In a wider-than-deep house the front center mezzanine rescues the seat selection by giving you the one thing center orchestra can't: altitude to take in the full 44'10" proscenium at once. Multiple patrons specifically cite this row range for Mamma Mia! and BTTF over the rear orchestra, and it avoids both the pillar risk on the sides and the mezz overhang clipping rear stalls.

Wide-house geometry pushes the far-left and far-right mezz off at a sharp angle — the stage-opposite corner is the consistent casualty. Reviewers note the speaker stacks on the edge as a recurring blocker, and because the mezz is only ~9 rows deep, distance isn't the killer — angle is. Good option if you're watching a show where the action centers; poor for full-stage choreography.

sg.n: Box Seats (Box B, C, F, G)
sg.ra: The Winter Garden boxes are widely flagged as among the most obstructed in Broadway — the box structure itself blocks significant stage area and the side angle compounds it. Skip at any price.
